title: SG-1.3 Selecting Lean Six Sigma Projects

1.3.1.examLens: Most questions ask you to spot what is wrong with a charter (a problem statement that already contains the solution, a goal that is not measurable, a scope that is too big) or to choose between projects.

worked.question:
Which problem statement is best?
(A) We need to install a new scheduling system to fix late shipments.
(B) Late shipments are caused by poor communication between planning and the warehouse.
(C) Between January and March, 22% of orders at the Memphis warehouse shipped after the promised date, compared with a 10% target.
(D) Shipping is too slow and customers are unhappy.
worked.solution: (C). It states what, where, when, and how big, and it names no cause or solution. (A) contains a solution. (B) contains a cause. (D) is vague and has no data.

1.3.2.examLens: Choose the right primary metric, notice when an improvement could cause harm somewhere else, and recognize which metrics lead and which lag.

worked.question: A hospital lab project cuts average test turnaround from 6 hours to 4 hours. Name a primary metric and a good balancing metric, and say whether each is leading or lagging.
worked.solution: Primary: turnaround time (continuous). It is a process metric and can be tracked in real time, so it is leading relative to patient outcomes. A good balancing metric is the rate of reporting errors (or retest rate), because speed could increase mistakes. It is lagging, since errors are found afterward.

1.3.3.examLens: Classify benefits as hard or soft, do simple ROI and payback arithmetic, and decide which project to fund.

worked.question: Project A costs $40,000 and saves $60,000 per year in scrap (hard savings). Project B costs $100,000 and avoids $80,000 per year in expected overtime (cost avoidance, soft). (a) Payback for each. (b) First-year ROI for each. (c) Which should be funded first?
worked.solution:
(a) A: 40,000 ÷ 60,000 = 0.67 years (about 8 months). B: 100,000 ÷ 80,000 = 1.25 years.
(b) A: (60,000 − 40,000) ÷ 40,000 = +50%. B: (80,000 − 100,000) ÷ 100,000 = −20% in the first year.
(c) Project A. It pays back faster, returns positive ROI in year one, and its benefit is hard cash.

1.3.1.a.title: Charter elements
1.3.1.a.html:
The charter is the agreement between the team and the sponsor. It normally contains:

  • Business case: why the project matters, in strategic and financial terms.
  • Problem statement: what is wrong, where, when, and how big.
  • Goal statement: the target, with a baseline and a deadline.
  • Scope: what is in and what is out.
  • Timeline: phase dates and milestones.
  • Team and roles: who does what, including the sponsor and champion.
  • Resources: people, budget, and time the team can draw on.
  • Constraints and assumptions: limits the team must work within and things taken as true.
  • Risks: what could derail the project.
  • Sign-off: the sponsor's approval.

1.3.1.b.title: The problem statement
1.3.1.b.html:
A good problem statement says what is wrong, where, when, and how big the gap is. It contains no cause, no solution, and no blame.
Good: "In Q2, 14% of invoices from the Dallas billing center were issued with errors, up from 6% a year ago."
Bad: "We need new billing software because the staff keep making mistakes." (It names a solution and blames people.)
Stating a cause or solution too early closes off the investigation before the data has spoken.

1.3.1.c.title: The goal statement
1.3.1.c.html:
The goal is SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. It names the baseline, the target, and the date.
Example: "Reduce the invoice error rate from 14% to 5% by December 31."
Check three things: is there a number, is there a baseline, and is there a deadline?

1.3.1.d.title: Scope
1.3.1.d.html:
Scope lists what is in scope and out of scope.

  • Scope creep is work added after the project starts, with no change in time or resources.
  • A project that tries to fix everything is "boiling the ocean." It is too big to finish and has no chance of a clear result.

Fix an oversized project by narrowing to one process, one site, or one defect type, and moving the rest to a later phase.

1.3.1.e.title: Stakeholders, RACI, and communication
1.3.1.e.html:
• Stakeholder analysis identifies who is affected, how much influence they have, and whether they support or resist the change.
  • RACI assigns each task: Responsible (does the work), Accountable (owns the result; one person per task), Consulted (gives input), Informed (told the outcome).
  • A communication plan says who gets what information, how often, and by what channel.

1.3.1.f.title: Project selection and alignment
1.3.1.f.html:
Not every problem deserves a project. Good projects line up with company strategy, have a measurable benefit, and are doable with the resources available. An impact/effort matrix plots projects on a grid: high impact and low effort go first, and low impact with high effort usually does not get done.
This is judgment-level (Evaluate) material, so expect questions that make you choose between candidate projects.

1.3.1.g.title: Spot the flawed problem statement
1.3.1.g.html: If a statement includes a solution ("we need new software"), a cause ("because operators are careless"), or no data (no size, place, or time), it is flawed. The correct fix is to rewrite it as the observed gap only.

1.3.2.a.title: Primary, secondary, and balancing metrics
1.3.2.a.html:
• Primary metric: the Y the project exists to move.
  • Secondary metrics: supporting measures that help explain the Y.
  • Consequential (balancing) metrics: watch for harm elsewhere. They guard against sub-optimization, where one measure improves while another gets worse.

Example: a project reduces call handling time (primary). A balancing metric is customer satisfaction, because rushed calls could lower it.

1.3.2.b.title: Definition, baseline, target, data type
1.3.2.b.html:
Every metric needs:

  • an operational definition: exactly how it is measured (see 1.2.2.e)
  • a baseline: where it is now
  • a target: where it should be, and by when
  • a data type: continuous (measured, such as time) or discrete (counted or classified, such as pass/fail). This choice later drives which statistical tools and control charts you can use.

1.3.2.c.title: Process versus outcome, leading versus lagging
1.3.2.c.html:
• Process metrics measure how the work is done (cycle time, first-pass yield). Outcome metrics measure the result the customer sees (on-time delivery, satisfaction).
  • Leading metrics move first and predict the result. Lagging metrics confirm it afterward.

Process metrics tend to be leading. Outcome metrics tend to be lagging.

1.3.2.d.title: Typical metrics
1.3.2.d.html: DPMO and defect rates (quality), yield (process success), cycle time (speed), COPQ (cost), Cpk (capability), and customer satisfaction (outcome). Pick the one that directly measures the problem in your problem statement.

1.3.2.e.title: Speed that hurts quality
1.3.2.e.html: If a project speeds up a process, quality may drop. The balancing metric exists to catch this. When a scenario says "the team cut cycle time by 30%," look for what the team did not measure.

1.3.3.a.title: Hard versus soft savings
1.3.3.a.html:
• Hard savings are real cash that shows up on the profit and loss statement: lower material cost, less scrap, fewer overtime hours paid.
  • Soft savings are real but do not directly change the books: cost avoidance, freed-up capacity, productivity, better customer satisfaction.

Finance cares most about hard savings.

1.3.3.b.title: Revenue growth, cost reduction, cost avoidance
1.3.3.b.html: Three ways a project creates value: revenue growth (more sales), cost reduction (spend goes down), and cost avoidance (spend that would have happened does not).

1.3.3.c.title: ROI
1.3.3.c.html:
ROI = (benefit − cost) ÷ cost.
Example: benefit $150,000, cost $50,000. ROI = (150,000 − 50,000) ÷ 50,000 = 2.0, or 200%.

1.3.3.d.title: Payback period
1.3.3.d.html:
Payback = investment ÷ annual benefit. The result is in years, and it assumes the net benefit is roughly the same every year. If cash flows are uneven, add them up year by year until the total reaches the investment.
Example: investment $60,000, annual benefit $40,000. Payback = 1.5 years.

1.3.3.e.title: NPV and IRR
1.3.3.e.html: Extension, glossary only. Net present value (NPV) discounts future cash to today's dollars. Internal rate of return (IRR) is the discount rate that makes NPV equal zero. Low exam yield.

1.3.3.f.title: Finance validation and benefit tracking
1.3.3.f.html: Extension. Many companies have finance sign off on savings and track benefits for about a year after the project. That is common practice, not an IASSC rule.

1.3.3.g.title: Classify, compute, decide
1.3.3.g.html: Typical question: read the project data, classify the benefit, compute payback or ROI, and choose which to fund. Shorter payback and higher ROI usually win, but check whether the benefit is hard or soft.

options.html: We need to buy a new CRM system to fix our slow order entry.
Order entry errors are caused by poor training.
During July, 9% of orders at the Reno center contained entry errors, compared with a 2% target.
Our order entry process is bad and customers are upset.

1.3.1-1.explanation: It states what, where, when, and how big, with no cause or solution. (A) contains a solution, (B) contains a cause, and (D) is vague with no data.

options.html: Improve invoice accuracy as much as possible.
Reduce invoice errors from 8% to 3% by December 31 at the Dallas billing center.
Make billing the best in the company.
Cut errors soon with help from the team.

1.3.1-2.explanation: It has a baseline, a target, a deadline, and a location, so it is specific and measurable.

1.3.1-3.stem: A team charters a project on late shipments at one warehouse. Midway through, the sponsor asks them to also fix returns processing, supplier quality, and two more warehouses, with no extra time or people. This is an example of:
1.3.1-3.explanation: Work was added after the project started without a change in time or resources.

1.3.1-4.stem: In a RACI chart, a single task may have several people who are Accountable.
1.3.1-4.explanation: Each task has exactly one Accountable person. Several people can be Responsible, Consulted, or Informed.

1.3.1-5.stem: A team is choosing among three candidate projects. P1 has high impact and low effort. P2 has high impact and high effort. P3 has low impact and low effort. Using an impact/effort matrix, which should the team start with?

options.html: All three at the same time

1.3.1-5.explanation: High impact with low effort is the best return for the resources available.

1.3.1-6.stem: Which TWO items belong in a project charter?
1.3.1-6.explanation: The root cause and the solution are discovered later in the project. The charter defines the problem and scope.

1.3.2-1.stem: A project cut average order-processing time by 35%, but the rate of order errors doubled. Which type of metric would have caught this?
1.3.2-1.explanation: A balancing metric watches for harm elsewhere, such as speed improving at the cost of quality.

options.html: Pass or fail of a weld
The number of defects on a circuit board
Time to resolve a support ticket, in minutes

1.3.2-2.explanation: Time is measured and can take any value. The others are counts, classifications, or ordered categories.

options.html: The hourly first-pass yield at a workstation
Hours of operator training completed this week

1.3.2-3.explanation: Satisfaction and warranty claims confirm results after the fact. First-pass yield and training hours are process or input measures that move first.

1.3.2-4.stem: A project's problem statement is "late deliveries." Which is the best primary metric?
1.3.2-4.explanation: The primary metric is the Y that directly measures the problem.

options.html: Reduced raw material purchases confirmed by finance
Avoided future overtime that was never budgeted
Freed capacity with no change in headcount

1.3.3-1.explanation: Hard benefits are cash that shows up in the financial statements. The others are soft benefits.

1.3.3-2.stem: An improvement removes the need for overtime that would have been spent next year. Nobody had budgeted it. This is:
1.3.3-2.explanation: Spending that would have happened but no longer will is cost avoidance. It does not reduce the current budget.

1.3.3-3.stem: A project costs $30,000 and delivers $90,000 in benefits. What is the ROI?

1.3.3-4.stem: A project requires a $45,000 investment and saves $30,000 per year. What is the payback period?

1.3.3-5.stem: Only one of two projects can be funded. Project A costs $50,000 and saves $70,000 per year in hard savings. Project B costs $80,000 and saves $70,000 per year in hard savings. Which should be funded, and why?

options.html: Project A, because it pays back in about 9 months versus about 14 months
Project B, because it costs more
Project A, because it costs less, regardless of savings
Neither, because the savings are equal

1.3.3-5.explanation: Payback A = 50,000 ÷ 70,000 = 0.71 years (about 9 months). Payback B = 80,000 ÷ 70,000 = 1.14 years (about 14 months). The annual savings are equal, so the lower investment and faster payback win.

1.3.3-17.answer: Payback A = 0.83 years, B = 1.00 years. First-year ROI A = 20%, B = 0%. Choose Project A, which pays back faster.
